finding.claim: Mass assignment on PUT /me lets any authenticated user overwrite arbitrary fields of their user record (conditional on the model having privilege-bearing fields such as role, isAdmin, or id). Severity HIGH on stated precondition; LOW if the model has no such fields.
finding.source: req.body in PUT /me, sent by any authenticated user
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) at users.js:5, then req.store.save(req.user) at users.js:6

trace.note: router.put('/me') handler registered with no authorization or field check
Object.assign copies every own key of req.body onto req.user
req.store.save persists the mutated user object
res.json(req.user) echoes the mutated record back to the attacker

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, schema validation, or key filtering in users.js. Auth middleware that sets req.user is not in the repo and cannot be verified. Prototype-chain variant: a __proto__ key invokes the __proto__ setter on req.user (per-object prototype change, not global pollution); impact depends on whether authorization reads inherited properties (unverified). Repro: PUT /me with {"role":"admin"} and check echoed body and an admin-gated route. Validation tier 0 once field names are known.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:5 copies every key of req.body onto req.user with Object.assign, with no allowlist or schema check, and users.js:6 persists the result. Auth middleware that sets req.user and any model-level field restriction are not in the repo, so they could not be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: users.js:4 registers PUT /me with no field filtering, users.js:5 applies all of req.body to req.user, users.js:6 saves it, and users.js:7 echoes it back. Any authenticated caller can therefore write arbitrary keys to their own record. Severity is conditional, since the impact depends on whether the user model has privilege-bearing fields that the repo does not show, so the candidate's HIGH-if-role-exists rating is unverified. The __proto__ variant also holds at the language level, because Object.assign uses [[Set]] and triggers the setter on req.user, but its authorization impact is unverified.

finding.claim: Partial profile update erases unspecified fields: Object.assign copies undefined values, so a body without displayName sets it to undefined and it is persisted. Self-affecting only, LOW.
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, { displayName, bio }) at users.js:12, then req.store.save at users.js:13

trace.note: destructure displayName and bio from req.body; absent keys become undefined
Object.assign copies undefined-valued properties onto req.user

finding.guards_checked: No undefined check. Impact confined to the requesting user's own record (triage Check 10, self-affecting), so LOW.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js. No undefined check exists at lines 11-13. The mechanism is accurate: line 11 destructures absent keys as undefined, line 12 Object.assign copies those undefined values onto req.user, and line 13 saves the record.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (users.js:11-13), but the attacker is an authenticated user changing only their own record, and that user already has write authority over displayName and bio, so this is a self-affecting functional bug rather than a security vulnerability.

finding.claim: displayName and bio are stored without type or length validation. Stored XSS for other users is possible only if a view renders them unescaped; that view is not in the repo. Held at LOW pending render-site review.
finding.sink: Object.assign at users.js:12 and req.store.save at users.js:13; downstream render sinks not in repo

trace.note: unvalidated destructure of request body fields

finding.guards_checked: No type, length, or output-escaping control in users.js. Escaping in views unverifiable. Re-rate to HIGH (tier 1) if an unescaped render of another user's profile is found.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js. No type, length, or escaping control is applied at users.js:11-13. Any output escaping would live in render code outside this repo, which contains only users.js and skill docs.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: users.js:11 destructures req.body.displayName and req.body.bio, users.js:12 assigns them onto req.user with Object.assign, and users.js:13 persists them via req.store.save. The stored-XSS impact depends on a render sink that is not in the repo, so the candidate's own LOW rating stands and the verdict cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Full user record is echoed in responses, which may expose credential material or other sensitive model fields to the requesting user. Self-affecting unless the record holds other users' secrets; LOW.
finding.source: Stored user record loaded into req.user (outside this file)

trace.note: PUT /me responds with the entire req.user object
PUT /me/profile responds with the entire req.user object

finding.guards_checked: No response DTO or field allowlist. Model schema not in repo, so presence of password hash or token fields is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. users.js:7 and users.js:14 call res.json(req.user) directly with no response DTO or field allowlist. The only other write-side code, Object.assign at users.js:5 and :12, is not a response guard.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: users.js:7 and users.js:14 both return the full req.user, and no guard sits between an authenticated caller and that response. Whether this is a vulnerability depends on fields in the user model, which is not in this repo, so I cannot tell whether the record holds credential material beyond the caller's own data.

finding.claim: req.store.save is not awaited and its result is not checked, so the client receives a success-shaped response before persistence is confirmed; an async rejection becomes unhandled. LOW reliability and logic gap.
finding.source: Any successful PUT /me or PUT /me/profile request
finding.sink: req.store.save at users.js:6 and users.js:13, followed by res.json

trace.note: save invoked without await or error handling
success response sent regardless of save outcome
success response sent regardless of save outcome

finding.guards_checked: No await, catch, or status check. Store implementation not in repo; impact depends on whether save is async or can fail.

verdict.guard_found: none. No await, try/catch, or status check wraps req.store.save at users.js:6 or users.js:13. The store implementation is not in the repo, so whether save is async or can reject is unknown.
verdict.reason: The trace matches users.js:6-7 and 13-14: save is called without await or error handling and res.json always follows, but whether this is a real defect depends on the store's save, which is not in the repo, and the only party affected is the authenticated user writing their own record (no security impact shown).
